description: Hand-labelled benchmark for scoring regressions. Within each group, takes answer the same prompt and are ranked by an experienced human coach: strong > medium > weak. Expectations are deliberately coarse (orderings, framework parts, verdict bands) so they test what matters, not exact numbers.

cases.prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a senior stakeholder.
cases.transcript: When I was leading the streaming platform migration last year, my director disagreed with my plan to move to Flink. My role was to deliver the migration by Q3. I decided to run a two week proof of concept and I shared the latency data with him. As a result we reduced latency by 40 percent and he approved the plan. I learned that data wins disagreements better than opinions.

cases.prompt: Describe a project that failed or slipped. What was your part in it?
cases.transcript: In my last role our payments launch slipped by three weeks. I owned the integration with the bank's API, and I underestimated their certification process. I set up a daily check-in with their team, I split the work so we could certify in two phases, and we launched the first phase two weeks later. As a result we kept 80 percent of the planned revenue that quarter. What I learned is to ask about certification on day one.

cases.prompt: Explain what a cache is to a product manager.
cases.transcript: In simple terms, a cache is a short-term memory for data. Think of keeping your most-used spices on the counter instead of in the basement. It works by saving the answer the first time, then serving the saved copy on the next request. The trade-off is that users sometimes see data that's a few minutes old, so we don't cache prices.

cases.prompt: What is one habit that changed your life?
cases.transcript: Have you ever counted how many minutes you lose to your phone before breakfast? Three years ago, I counted forty. My message is simple: protect your first hour. I remember the first morning I left my phone in the kitchen. I read ten pages, I walked, and I started work calm. So next time you reach for your phone at seven a.m., remember: the first hour is yours.

cases.prompt: A customer says your platform is too expensive compared to building in-house. Respond.
cases.transcript: I understand, cost matters and building in-house can look cheaper. What I'm hearing is that your concern is total cost this year. I recommend we compare the full cost: in-house needs about three engineers for a year, which is roughly six hundred thousand dollars. The risk with our platform is lock-in, and we mitigate that with standard export formats. As a next step, I'll send a cost comparison by Friday and we can review it together.
